{{Short description|Solution to a specific type of stochastic differential equation}}
{{no footnotes|date=July 2013}}
In [[mathematics]] – specifically, in [[stochastic processes|stochastic analysis]] – an '''Itô diffusion''' is a solution to a specific type of [[stochastic differential equation]]. That equation is similar to the [[Langevin equation]] used in [[physics]] to describe the [[Brownian motion]] of a particle subjected to a potential in a [[Viscosity|viscous]] fluid.  Itô diffusions are named after the [[Japan]]ese [[mathematician]] [[Kiyosi Itô]].

==Overview==
[[File:Wiener process 3d.png|thumb|250px|This [[Wiener process]] (Brownian motion) in three-dimensional space (one sample path shown) is an example of an Itô diffusion.]]

A ('''time-homogeneous''') '''Itô diffusion''' in ''n''-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] <math>\boldsymbol{\textbf{R}}^n</math> is a [[Stochastic process|process]] ''X''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞)&nbsp;×&nbsp;Ω&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> defined on a [[probability space]] (Ω,&nbsp;Σ,&nbsp;'''P''') and satisfying a stochastic differential equation of the form

:<math>\mathrm{d} X_{t} = b(X_t) \, \mathrm{d} t + \sigma (X_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} B_{t},</math>

where ''B'' is an ''m''-dimensional [[Brownian motion]] and ''b''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> and σ&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''×''m''</sup> satisfy the usual [[Lipschitz continuity]] condition

:<math>| b(x) - b(y) | + | \sigma (x) - \sigma (y) | \leq C | x - y |</math>

for some constant ''C'' and all ''x'', ''y'' ∈ '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>; this condition ensures the existence of a unique [[Stochastic differential equation#Use in probability and mathematical finance|strong solution]] ''X'' to the stochastic differential equation given above. The [[vector field]] ''b'' is known as the '''[[Stochastic drift|drift]] coefficient''' of ''X''; the [[tensor field|matrix field]] σ is known as the '''diffusion coefficient''' of ''X''. ''b'' and σ do not depend upon time; if they were, ''X'' would be referred to only as an ''[[Itô process]]'', not a diffusion. Itô diffusions have a number of nice properties, which include

* [[sample continuous process|sample]] and [[Feller-continuous process|Feller continuity]];
* the [[Markov property]];
* the [[strong Markov property]];
* the existence of an [[Infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)|infinitesimal generator]];
* the existence of a [[#The characteristic operator|characteristic operator]];
* [[Dynkin's formula]].

In particular, an Itô diffusion is a continuous, strongly Markovian process such that the domain of its characteristic operator includes all [[smooth function|twice-continuously differentiable]] functions, so it is a ''diffusion'' in the sense defined by Dynkin (1965).

==Continuity==
{{main|Continuous stochastic process}}

===Sample continuity===
An Itô diffusion ''X'' is a [[sample continuous process]], i.e., for [[almost all]] realisations ''B<sub>t</sub>''(ω) of the noise, ''X<sub>t</sub>''(ω) is a [[continuous function]] of the time parameter, ''t''. More accurately, there is a "continuous version" of ''X'', a continuous process ''Y'' so that

:<math>\mathbf{P} [ X_t = Y_t] = 1 \mbox{ for all } t.</math>

This follows from the standard existence and uniqueness theory for strong solutions of stochastic differential equations.

===Feller continuity===
In addition to being (sample) continuous, an Itô diffusion ''X'' satisfies the stronger requirement to be a [[Feller-continuous process]].

For a point ''x''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>, let '''P'''<sup>''x''</sup> denote the law of ''X'' given initial datum ''X''<sub>0</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x'', and let '''E'''<sup>''x''</sup> denote [[Expected value|expectation]] with respect to '''P'''<sup>''x''</sup>.

Let ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' be a [[Borel sigma algebra|Borel]]-[[measurable function]] that is [[bounded function|bounded below]] and define, for fixed ''t''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0, ''u''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' by

:<math>u(x) = \mathbf{E}^{x}[ f(X_t) ].</math>

* [[Semi-continuity|Lower semi-continuity]]: if ''f'' is lower semi-continuous, then ''u'' is lower semi-continuous.
* Feller continuity: if ''f'' is bounded and continuous, then ''u'' is continuous.

The behaviour of the function ''u'' above when the time ''t'' is varied is addressed by the Kolmogorov backward equation, the Fokker–Planck equation, etc. (See below.)

==The Markov property==
{{main|Markov property}}

===The Markov property===
An Itô diffusion ''X'' has the important property of being ''Markovian'': the future behaviour of ''X'', given what has happened up to some time ''t'', is the same as if the process had been started at the position ''X<sub>t</sub>'' at time 0. The precise mathematical formulation of this statement requires some additional notation:

Let Σ<sub>∗</sub> denote the [[natural filtration|natural]] [[filtration (abstract algebra)|filtration]] of (Ω,&nbsp;Σ) generated by the Brownian motion ''B'': for ''t''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0,

:<math>\Sigma_{t} = \Sigma_{t}^{B} = \sigma \left \{ B_{s}^{-1} (A) \subseteq \Omega \ : \ 0 \leq s \leq t, A \subseteq \mathbf{R}^{n} \mbox{ Borel} \right\}.</math>

It is easy to show that ''X'' is [[adapted process|adapted]] to Σ<sub>∗</sub> (i.e. each ''X<sub>t</sub>'' is Σ<sub>''t''</sub>-measurable), so the natural filtration ''F''<sub>∗</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''F''<sub>∗</sub><sup>''X''</sup> of (Ω,&nbsp;Σ) generated by ''X'' has ''F<sub>t</sub>''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;Σ<sub>''t''</sub> for each ''t''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0.

Let ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' be a bounded, Borel-measurable function. Then, for all ''t'' and ''h''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0, the [[conditional expectation]] conditioned on the [[Sigma-algebra|σ-algebra]] Σ<sub>''t''</sub> and the expectation of the process "restarted" from ''X<sub>t</sub>'' satisfy the '''Markov property''':

:<math>\mathbf{E}^{x} \big[ f(X_{t+h}) \big| \Sigma_{t} \big] (\omega) = \mathbf{E}^{X_{t} (\omega)}[ f(X_{h})].</math>

In fact, ''X'' is also a Markov process with respect to the filtration ''F''<sub>∗</sub>, as the following shows:

:<math>\begin{align}
\mathbf{E}^{x} \left [ f(X_{t+h}) \big| F_{t} \right ] &= \mathbf{E}^{x} \left [ \mathbf{E}^{x} \left [ f(X_{t+h}) \big| \Sigma_{t} \right] \big| F_{t} \right] \\
&= \mathbf{E}^{x} \left [ \mathbf{E}^{X_{t}} \left [ f(X_{h}) \right] \big| F_{t} \right] \\
&= \mathbf{E}^{X_{t}} \left [ f(X_{h}) \right ].
\end{align}</math>

===The strong Markov property===
The strong Markov property is a generalization of the Markov property above in which ''t'' is replaced by a suitable random time τ&nbsp;:&nbsp;Ω&nbsp;→&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞] known as a [[stopping time]]. So, for example, rather than "restarting" the process ''X'' at time ''t''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1, one could "restart" whenever ''X'' first reaches some specified point ''p'' of '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>.

As before, let ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' be a bounded, Borel-measurable function. Let τ be a stopping time with respect to the filtration Σ<sub>∗</sub> with τ&nbsp;<&nbsp;+∞ [[almost surely]]. Then, for all ''h''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0,

:<math>\mathbf{E}^{x} \big[ f(X_{\tau+h}) \big| \Sigma_{\tau} \big] = \mathbf{E}^{X_{\tau}} \big[ f(X_{h}) \big].</math>

==The generator==
{{main|Infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)}}

===Definition===
Associated to each Itô diffusion, there is a second-order [[partial differential operator]] known as the ''generator'' of the diffusion. The generator is very useful in many applications and encodes a great deal of information about the process ''X''. Formally, the '''infinitesimal generator''' of an Itô diffusion ''X'' is the operator ''A'', which is defined to act on suitable functions ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' by

:<math>A f (x) = \lim_{t \downarrow 0} \frac{\mathbf{E}^{x} [f(X_{t})] - f(x)}{t}.</math>

The set of all functions ''f'' for which this limit exists at a point ''x'' is denoted ''D<sub>A</sub>''(''x''), while ''D<sub>A</sub>'' denotes the set of all ''f'' for which the limit exists for all ''x''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>. One can show that any [[compact support|compactly-supported]] ''C''<sup>2</sup> (twice differentiable with continuous second derivative) function ''f'' lies in ''D<sub>A</sub>'' and that

:<math>Af(x) = \sum_{i} b_{i} (x) \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} (x) + \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i, j} \left( \sigma (x) \sigma (x)^{\top} \right)_{i, j} \frac{\partial^{2} f}{\partial x_i \, \partial x_{j}} (x),</math>

or, in terms of the [[gradient]] and [[dot product|scalar]] and [[Frobenius inner product|Frobenius]] [[inner product]]s,

:<math>A f (x) = b(x) \cdot \nabla_{x} f(x) + \tfrac1{2} \left( \sigma(x) \sigma(x)^{\top} \right ) : \nabla_{x} \nabla_{x} f(x).</math>

===An example===
The generator ''A'' for standard ''n''-dimensional Brownian motion ''B'', which satisfies the stochastic differential equation d''X<sub>t</sub>''&nbsp;=&nbsp;d''B<sub>t</sub>'', is given by

:<math>A f (x) = \tfrac1{2} \sum_{i, j} \delta_{ij} \frac{\partial^{2} f}{\partial x_{i} \, \partial x_{j}} (x) = \tfrac1{2} \sum_{i} \frac{\partial^{2} f}{\partial x_{i}^{2}} (x)</math>,

i.e., ''A''&nbsp;=&nbsp;Δ/2, where Δ denotes the [[Laplace operator]].

===The Kolmogorov and Fokker–Planck equations===
{{main|Kolmogorov backward equation|Fokker–Planck equation}}

The generator is used in the formulation of Kolmogorov's backward equation. Intuitively, this equation tells us how the expected value of any suitably smooth statistic of ''X'' evolves in time: it must solve a certain [[partial differential equation]] in which time ''t'' and the initial position ''x'' are the independent variables. More precisely, if ''f''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''C''<sup>2</sup>('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>;&nbsp;'''R''') has compact support and ''u''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞)&nbsp;×&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' is defined by

:<math>u(t, x) = \mathbf{E}^{x} [ f(X_t)],</math>

then ''u''(''t'',&nbsp;''x'') is differentiable with respect to ''t'', ''u''(''t'',&nbsp;·)&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''D<sub>A</sub>'' for all ''t'', and ''u'' satisfies the following [[partial differential equation]], known as '''Kolmogorov's backward equation''':

:<math>\begin{cases} \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t}(t, x) = A u (t, x), & t > 0, x \in \mathbf{R}^{n}; \\ u(0, x) = f(x), & x \in \mathbf{R}^{n}. \end{cases}</math>

The Fokker–Planck equation (also known as ''Kolmogorov's forward equation'') is in some sense the "[[adjoint]]" to the backward equation, and tells us how the [[probability density function]]s of ''X<sub>t</sub>'' evolve with time ''t''. Let ρ(''t'',&nbsp;·) be the density of ''X<sub>t</sub>'' with respect to [[Lebesgue measure]] on '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>, i.e., for any Borel-measurable set ''S''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>,

:<math>\mathbf{P} \left [ X_t \in S \right ] = \int_{S} \rho(t, x) \, \mathrm{d} x.</math>

Let ''A''<sup>∗</sup> denote the [[Hermitian adjoint]] of ''A'' (with respect to the [[Lp space|''L''<sup>2</sup>]] [[inner product]]). Then, given that the initial position ''X''<sub>0</sub> has a prescribed density ρ<sub>0</sub>, ρ(''t'',&nbsp;''x'') is differentiable with respect to ''t'', ρ(''t'',&nbsp;·)&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''D<sub>A</sub>''<sub>*</sub> for all ''t'', and ρ satisfies the following partial differential equation, known as the '''Fokker–Planck equation''':

:<math>\begin{cases} \dfrac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}(t, x) = A^{*} \rho (t, x), & t > 0, x \in \mathbf{R}^{n}; \\ \rho(0, x) = \rho_{0} (x), & x \in \mathbf{R}^{n}. \end{cases}</math>

===The Feynman–Kac formula===
{{main|Feynman–Kac formula}}

The Feynman–Kac formula is a useful generalization of Kolmogorov's backward equation. Again, ''f'' is in ''C''<sup>2</sup>('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>;&nbsp;'''R''') and has compact support, and ''q''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' is taken to be a [[continuous function]] that is bounded below. Define a function ''v''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞)&nbsp;×&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' by

:<math>v(t, x) = \mathbf{E}^{x} \left[ \exp \left( - \int_{0}^{t} q(X_{s}) \, \mathrm{d} s \right) f(X_{t}) \right].</math>

The '''Feynman–Kac formula''' states that ''v'' satisfies the partial differential equation

:<math>\begin{cases} \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial t}(t, x) = A v (t, x) - q(x) v(t, x), & t > 0, x \in \mathbf{R}^{n}; \\ v(0, x) = f(x), & x \in \mathbf{R}^{n}. \end{cases}</math>

Moreover, if ''w''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞)&nbsp;×&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' is ''C''<sup>1</sup> in time, ''C''<sup>2</sup> in space, bounded on ''K''&nbsp;×&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> for all compact ''K'', and satisfies the above partial differential equation, then ''w'' must be ''v'' as defined above.

Kolmogorov's backward equation is the special case of the Feynman–Kac formula in which ''q''(''x'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 for all ''x''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>.

==The characteristic operator==

===Definition===
The [[characteristic operator]] of an Itô diffusion ''X'' is a partial differential operator closely related to the generator, but somewhat more general. It is more suited to certain problems, for example in the solution of the [[Dirichlet problem]].

The '''characteristic operator''' <math>\mathcal{A}</math> of an Itô diffusion ''X'' is defined by

:<math>\mathcal{A} f (x) = \lim_{U \downarrow x} \frac{\mathbf{E}^{x} \left [ f(X_{\tau_{U}}) \right ] - f(x)}{\mathbf{E}^{x} [\tau_{U}]},</math>

where the sets ''U'' form a sequence of [[open set]]s ''U<sub>k</sub>'' that decrease to the point ''x'' in the sense that

:<math>U_{k + 1} \subseteq U_{k} \mbox{ and } \bigcap_{k = 1}^{\infty} U_{k} = \{ x \},</math>

and

:<math>\tau_{U} = \inf \{ t \geq 0 \ : \ X_{t} \not \in U \}</math>

is the first exit time from ''U'' for ''X''. <math>D_{\mathcal{A}}</math> denotes the set of all ''f'' for which this limit exists for all ''x''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> and all sequences {''U<sub>k</sub>''}. If '''E'''<sup>''x''</sup>[τ<sub>''U''</sub>]&nbsp;=&nbsp;+∞ for all open sets ''U'' containing ''x'', define

:<math>\mathcal{A} f (x) = 0.</math>

===Relationship with the generator===
The characteristic operator and infinitesimal generator are very closely related, and even agree for a large class of functions. One can show that

:<math>D_{A} \subseteq D_{\mathcal{A}}</math>

and that

:<math>A f = \mathcal{A} f \mbox{ for all } f \in D_{A}.</math>

In particular, the generator and characteristic operator agree for all ''C''<sup>2</sup> functions ''f'', in which case

:<math>\mathcal{A} f(x) = \sum_i b_i (x) \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}} (x) + \tfrac1{2} \sum_{i, j} \left( \sigma (x) \sigma (x)^{\top} \right)_{i, j} \frac{\partial^{2} f}{\partial x_{i} \, \partial x_{j}} (x).</math>

===Application: Brownian motion on a Riemannian manifold===

[[File:BMonSphere.jpg|thumb|The characteristic operator of a Brownian motion is {{sfrac|1|2}} times the Laplace-Beltrami operator. Here it is the Laplace-Beltrami operator on a 2-sphere.]]

Above, the generator (and hence characteristic operator) of Brownian motion on '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> was calculated to be {{sfrac|1|2}}Δ, where Δ denotes the Laplace operator. The characteristic operator is useful in defining Brownian motion on an ''m''-dimensional [[Riemannian manifold]] (''M'',&nbsp;''g''): a '''Brownian motion on''' ''M'' is defined to be a diffusion on ''M'' whose characteristic operator <math>\mathcal{A}</math> in local coordinates ''x<sub>i</sub>'', 1&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''i''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''m'', is given by {{sfrac|1|2}}Δ<sub>LB</sub>, where Δ<sub>LB</sub> is the [[Laplace operator#Laplace–Beltrami operator|Laplace-Beltrami operator]] given in local coordinates by

:<math>\Delta_{\mathrm{LB}} = \frac1{\sqrt{\det(g)}} \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}} \left( \sqrt{\det(g)} \sum_{j = 1}^{m} g^{ij} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{j}} \right),</math>

where [''g<sup>ij</sup>'']&nbsp;=&nbsp;[''g<sub>ij</sub>'']<sup>−1</sup> in the sense of [[Invertible matrix|the inverse of a square matrix]].

==The resolvent operator==
In general, the generator ''A'' of an Itô diffusion ''X'' is not a [[bounded operator]]. However, if a positive multiple of the identity operator '''I''' is subtracted from ''A'' then the resulting operator is invertible. The inverse of this operator can be expressed in terms of ''X'' itself using the [[Feller process#Resolvent|resolvent]] operator.

For α&nbsp;>&nbsp;0, the '''resolvent operator''' ''R''<sub>α</sub>, acting on bounded, continuous functions ''g''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''', is defined by

:<math>R_{\alpha} g (x) = \mathbf{E}^{x} \left[ \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{- \alpha t} g(X_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} t \right].</math>

It can be shown, using the Feller continuity of the diffusion ''X'', that ''R''<sub>α</sub>''g'' is itself a bounded, continuous function. Also, ''R''<sub>α</sub> and α'''I'''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''A'' are mutually inverse operators:
* if ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' is ''C''<sup>2</sup> with compact support, then, for all α&nbsp;>&nbsp;0,
::<math>R_{\alpha} (\alpha \mathbf{I} - A) f = f;</math>
* if ''g''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' is bounded and continuous, then ''R''<sub>α</sub>''g'' lies in ''D<sub>A</sub>'' and, for all α&nbsp;>&nbsp;0,
::<math>(\alpha \mathbf{I} - A) R_{\alpha} g = g.</math>

==Invariant measures==
Sometimes it is necessary to find an [[invariant measure]] for an Itô diffusion ''X'', i.e. a measure on '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> that does not change under the "flow" of ''X'': i.e., if ''X''<sub>0</sub> is distributed according to such an invariant measure μ<sub>∞</sub>, then ''X<sub>t</sub>'' is also distributed according to μ<sub>∞</sub> for any ''t''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0. The Fokker–Planck equation offers a way to find such a measure, at least if it has a probability density function ρ<sub>∞</sub>: if ''X''<sub>0</sub> is indeed distributed according to an invariant measure μ<sub>∞</sub> with density ρ<sub>∞</sub>, then the density ρ(''t'',&nbsp;·) of ''X<sub>t</sub>'' does not change with ''t'', so ρ(''t'',&nbsp;·)&nbsp;=&nbsp;ρ<sub>∞</sub>, and so ρ<sub>∞</sub> must solve the (time-independent) partial differential equation

:<math>A^{*} \rho_{\infty} (x) = 0, \quad x \in \mathbf{R}^{n}.</math>

This illustrates one of the connections between stochastic analysis and the study of partial differential equations. Conversely, a given second-order linear partial differential equation of the form Λ''f''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 may be hard to solve directly, but if Λ&nbsp;=&nbsp;''A''<sup>∗</sup> for some Itô diffusion ''X'', and an invariant measure for ''X'' is easy to compute, then that measure's density provides a solution to the partial differential equation.

===Invariant measures for gradient flows===
An invariant measure is comparatively easy to compute when the process ''X'' is a stochastic gradient flow of the form

:<math>\mathrm{d} X_{t} = - \nabla \Psi (X_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} t + \sqrt{2 \beta^{-1}} \, \mathrm{d} B_{t},</math>

where β&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 plays the role of an [[inverse temperature]] and Ψ&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' is a scalar potential satisfying suitable smoothness and growth conditions. In this case, the Fokker–Planck equation has a unique stationary solution ρ<sub>∞</sub> (i.e. ''X'' has a unique invariant measure μ<sub>∞</sub> with density ρ<sub>∞</sub>) and it is given by the [[Gibbs distribution]]:

:<math>\rho_{\infty} (x) = Z^{-1} \exp ( - \beta \Psi (x) ),</math>

where the [[partition function (statistical mechanics)|partition function]] ''Z'' is given by

:<math>Z = \int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}} \exp ( - \beta \Psi (x) ) \, \mathrm{d} x.</math>

Moreover, the density ρ<sub>∞</sub> satisfies a [[variational principle]]: it minimizes over all probability densities ρ on '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> the [[Thermodynamic free energy|free energy]] functional ''F'' given by

:<math>F[\rho] = E[\rho] + \frac1{\beta} S[\rho],</math>

where

:<math>E[\rho] = \int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}} \Psi(x) \rho(x) \, \mathrm{d} x</math>

plays the role of an energy functional, and

:<math>S[\rho] = \int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}} \rho(x) \log \rho(x) \, \mathrm{d} x</math>

is the negative of the Gibbs-Boltzmann entropy functional. Even when the potential Ψ is not well-behaved enough for the partition function ''Z'' and the Gibbs measure μ<sub>∞</sub> to be defined, the free energy ''F''[ρ(''t'',&nbsp;·)] still makes sense for each time ''t''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0, provided that the initial condition has ''F''[ρ(0,&nbsp;·)]&nbsp;<&nbsp;+∞. The free energy functional ''F'' is, in fact, a [[Lyapunov function]] for the Fokker–Planck equation: ''F''[ρ(''t'',&nbsp;·)] must decrease as ''t'' increases. Thus, ''F'' is an [[H-theorem|''H''-function]] for the ''X''-dynamics.

===Example===
Consider the [[Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process]] ''X'' on '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> satisfying the stochastic differential equation

:<math>\mathrm{d} X_{t} = -  \kappa ( X_{t} - m) \, \mathrm{d} t + \sqrt{2 \beta^{-1}} \, \mathrm{d} B_{t},</math>

where ''m''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> and β, κ&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 are given constants. In this case, the potential Ψ is given by

:<math>\Psi(x) = \tfrac{1}{2} \kappa |x - m|^2,</math>

and so the invariant measure for ''X'' is a [[Gaussian measure]] with density ρ<sub>∞</sub> given by

:<math>\rho_{\infty} (x) = \left( \frac{\beta \kappa}{2 \pi} \right)^{\frac{n}{2}} \exp \left( - \frac{\beta \kappa | x - m |^{2}}{2} \right)</math>.

Heuristically, for large ''t'', ''X<sub>t</sub>'' is approximately [[normal distribution|normally distributed]] with mean ''m'' and variance (βκ)<sup>−1</sup>. The expression for the variance may be interpreted as follows: large values of κ mean that the potential well Ψ has "very steep sides", so ''X<sub>t</sub>'' is unlikely to move far from the minimum of Ψ at ''m''; similarly, large values of β mean that the system is quite "cold" with little noise, so, again, ''X<sub>t</sub>'' is unlikely to move far away from ''m''.

==The martingale property==
In general, an Itô diffusion ''X'' is not a [[martingale (probability theory)|martingale]]. However, for any ''f''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''C''<sup>2</sup>('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>;&nbsp;'''R''') with compact support, the process ''M''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞)&nbsp;×&nbsp;Ω&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' defined by

:<math>M_{t} = f(X_{t}) - \int_{0}^{t} A f(X_{s}) \, \mathrm{d} s,</math>

where ''A'' is the generator of ''X'', is a martingale with respect to the natural filtration ''F''<sub>∗</sub> of (Ω,&nbsp;Σ) by ''X''. The proof is quite simple: it follows from the usual expression of the action of the generator on smooth enough functions ''f'' and [[Itô's lemma]] (the stochastic [[chain rule]]) that

:<math>f(X_{t}) = f(x) + \int_{0}^{t} A f(X_{s}) \, \mathrm{d} s + \int_{0}^{t} \nabla f(X_{s})^{\top} \sigma(X_{s}) \, \mathrm{d} B_{s}.</math>

Since Itô integrals are martingales with respect to the natural filtration Σ<sub>∗</sub> of (Ω,&nbsp;Σ) by ''B'', for ''t''&nbsp;>&nbsp;''s'',

:<math>\mathbf{E}^{x} \big[ M_{t} \big| \Sigma_{s} \big] = M_{s}.</math>

Hence, as required,

:<math>\mathbf{E}^{x}[M_t | F_s] = \mathbf{E}^{x} \left[ \mathbf{E}^{x} \big[ M_{t} \big| \Sigma_{s} \big] \big| F_{s} \right] = \mathbf{E}^{x} \big[ M_{s} \big| F_{s} \big] = M_{s},</math>

since ''M<sub>s</sub>'' is ''F<sub>s</sub>''-measurable.

==Dynkin's formula==
{{main|Dynkin's formula}}

Dynkin's formula, named after [[Eugene Dynkin]], gives the [[expected value]] of any suitably smooth statistic of an Itô diffusion ''X'' (with generator ''A'') at a stopping time. Precisely, if τ is a stopping time with '''E'''<sup>''x''</sup>[τ]&nbsp;<&nbsp;+∞, and ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' is ''C''<sup>2</sup> with compact support, then

:<math>\mathbf{E}^{x} [f(X_{\tau})] = f(x) + \mathbf{E}^{x} \left[ \int_{0}^{\tau} A f (X_{s}) \, \mathrm{d} s \right].</math>

Dynkin's formula can be used to calculate many useful statistics of stopping times. For example, canonical Brownian motion on the real line starting at 0 exits the [[interval (mathematics)|interval]] (−''R'',&nbsp;+''R'') at a random time τ<sub>''R''</sub> with expected value

:<math>\mathbf{E}^{0} [\tau_{R}] = R^{2}.</math>

Dynkin's formula provides information about the behaviour of ''X'' at a fairly general stopping time. For more information on the distribution of ''X'' at a [[hitting time]], one can study the ''harmonic measure'' of the process.

==Associated measures==

===The harmonic measure===
{{main|Harmonic measure}}

In many situations, it is sufficient to know when an Itô diffusion ''X'' will first leave a [[measurable set]] ''H''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>. That is, one wishes to study the [[hitting time|first exit time]]

:<math>\tau_{H} (\omega) = \inf \{ t \geq 0 | X_{t} \not \in H \}.</math>

Sometimes, however, one also wishes to know the distribution of the points at which ''X'' exits the set. For example, canonical Brownian motion ''B'' on the real line starting at 0 exits the [[interval (mathematics)|interval]] (−1,&nbsp;1) at −1 with probability {{sfrac|1|2}} and at 1 with probability {{sfrac|1|2}}, so ''B''<sub>τ<sub>(−1,&nbsp;1)</sub></sub> is [[uniform distribution (discrete)|uniformly distributed]] on the set {−1,&nbsp;1}.

In general, if ''G'' is [[compactly embedded]] within '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>, then the '''harmonic measure''' (or '''hitting distribution''') of ''X'' on the [[boundary (topology)|boundary]] ∂''G'' of ''G'' is the measure μ<sub>''G''</sub><sup>''x''</sup> defined by

:<math>\mu_{G}^{x} (F) = \mathbf{P}^{x} \left [ X_{\tau_{G}} \in F \right ]</math>

for ''x''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''G'' and ''F''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;∂''G''.

Returning to the earlier example of Brownian motion, one can show that if ''B'' is a Brownian motion in '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> starting at ''x''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> and ''D''&nbsp;⊂&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> is an [[open ball]] centred on ''x'', then the harmonic measure of ''B'' on ∂''D'' is [[invariant measure|invariant]] under all [[rotation]]s of ''D'' about ''x'' and coincides with the normalized [[surface measure]] on ∂''D''.

The harmonic measure satisfies an interesting '''mean value property''': if ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' is any bounded, Borel-measurable function and φ is given by

:<math>\varphi (x) = \mathbf{E}^{x} \left [ f(X_{\tau_{H}}) \right],</math>

then, for all Borel sets ''G''&nbsp;⊂⊂&nbsp;''H'' and all ''x''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''G'',

:<math>\varphi (x) = \int_{\partial G} \varphi (y) \, \mathrm{d} \mu_{G}^{x} (y).</math>

The mean value property is very useful in the [[Stochastic processes and boundary value problems|solution of partial differential equations using stochastic processes]].

===The Green measure and Green formula===
{{main|Green measure}}

Let ''A'' be a partial differential operator on a domain ''D''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> and let ''X'' be an Itô diffusion with ''A'' as its generator. Intuitively, the Green measure of a Borel set ''H'' is the expected length of time that ''X'' stays in ''H'' before it leaves the domain ''D''. That is, the '''Green measure''' of ''X'' with respect to ''D'' at ''x'', denoted ''G''(''x'',&nbsp;·), is defined for Borel sets ''H''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> by

:<math>G(x, H) = \mathbf{E}^{x} \left[ \int_{0}^{\tau_{D}} \chi_{H} (X_{s}) \, \mathrm{d} s \right],</math>

or for bounded, continuous functions ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;''D''&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R''' by

:<math>\int_{D} f(y) \, G(x, \mathrm{d} y) = \mathbf{E}^{x} \left[ \int_{0}^{\tau_{D}} f(X_{s}) \, \mathrm{d} s \right].</math>

The name "Green measure" comes from the fact that if ''X'' is Brownian motion, then

:<math>G(x, H) = \int_{H} G(x, y) \, \mathrm{d} y,</math>

where ''G''(''x'',&nbsp;''y'') is [[Green's function]] for the operator {{sfrac|1|2}}Δ on the domain ''D''.

Suppose that '''E'''<sup>''x''</sup>[τ<sub>''D''</sub>]&nbsp;<&nbsp;+∞ for all ''x''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''D''. Then the '''Green formula''' holds for all ''f''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''C''<sup>2</sup>('''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>;&nbsp;'''R''') with compact support:

:<math>f(x) = \mathbf{E}^{x} \left[ f \left( X_{\tau_{D}} \right) \right] - \int_{D} A f (y) \, G(x, \mathrm{d} y).</math>

In particular, if the support of ''f'' is [[compactly embedded]] in ''D'',

:<math>f(x) = - \int_{D} A f (y) \, G(x, \mathrm{d} y).</math>
